01

What was delivered

A trained surrogate, and the data pipeline that earns the right to trust it

Given a plate outline and a hole position, the model returns the full stress field in about 16 milliseconds — no meshing, no solver. It reproduces the finite-element answer to 1% of the applied nominal stress across the design space it was trained on.

The model itself is a standard UNet. What makes the result defensible is the pipeline underneath it: every one of the 545 training cases was generated by an agentic FEA workflow that gates each case on physics before it is allowed into the dataset — force balance, free-surface conditions, mesh quality — and six of them are cross-checked against a closed-form textbook solution to better than 1%. A surrogate is only as trustworthy as its labels, and these labels were audited case by case.

The ask

Design-space exploration

Engineers need peak stress for hundreds of hole positions per study. Each FEA run is cheap alone and expensive in bulk.

The approach

Learn the field, not the number

Predicting the whole field rather than a single factor keeps the result inspectable and lets us check it against physics the model never saw.

The catch

It has a domain

Inside its training envelope it is reliable. One step outside — a different plate proportion — and it fails confidently. Section 07 quantifies this.

02

The physical problem

Uniaxial tension of a finite plate containing a circular hole

A 200 × 100 × 1 mm steel plate is pulled along its length by a total force of 1000 N. A circular hole of radius r sits at position (xc, yc). The hole raises the local stress far above the nominal value; that concentration is what drives fatigue life, and it is what the surrogate has to get right.

The model as solved. Left edge on rollers (ux = 0, teal), a single anchor node fixing uy (red), and the load applied as consistent nodal forces along the right edge (orange). The support model is deliberately not a full clamp: clamping would forbid the Poisson contraction and manufacture a singular corner stress that never converges under mesh refinement — it would poison both the peak value and any field data taken from the run. Mesh is refined at the hole and across the thinnest ligament.
03

How the dataset was generated

545 cases · every one gated on physics before it became a label

Each case runs the full analysis chain. Four checks are blocking: a case that fails one is never exported, so bad data cannot reach the model by accident.

01
Mesh
Quadratic elements, refined at the hole and across the ligament
GATE
Mesh quality
No inverted elements; area matches a·b − πr² to <0.05%
02
Solve
CalculiX, plane stress, 0.39 s
GATE
Physics
Force balance, displacement direction, strain energy, free hole surface
AUDIT
Versus theory
Centred holes checked against Howland/Peterson
03
Export
Field sampled onto a fixed 384 × 192 grid

Result: 545 of 545 cases passed every gate. The five deliberately centred “anchor” cases — the only geometry with a closed-form answer — matched the Howland/Peterson reference to within 0.93% worst case, which is inside that reference’s own stated accuracy of about 1%.

Sampling

Three parameters, not six

Plate size, force and thickness are held fixed. Dimensional analysis says the normalised field depends only on the ratios r/b, xc/a, yc/b and a/b — and σ scales linearly with F/t, so force and thickness are free rescalings, not dimensions worth spending samples on.

Method

Conditional Latin hypercube

The feasible region is a wedge: a bigger hole has less room to move. Sampling a bounding box and rejecting what falls outside would have discarded a third of the budget and biased the survivors toward small holes. Instead r is stratified directly and the hole centre is drawn inside each radius’s own feasible box.

The design space, and what governs it. Left: the concentration factor tracks the thinnest remaining ligament (correlation −0.54), not the hole radius (−0.07). Right: coverage of the feasible wedge; marker size is the hole radius, so the narrowing band for large holes is the geometric constraint, not a sampling gap.
04

What goes in, what comes out

Two geometry channels → three stress channels, all dimensionless
Input · 2 × 192 × 384

mask  ·  signed distance field

mask is 1 where there is material, 0 in the hole and off the plate.

SDF gives every pixel its distance to the hole edge, divided by the plate width. A binary mask is flat everywhere except at the edge, so a pixel far from the hole looks identical to one close to it; the network could only recover distance by growing a receptive field large enough to see the hole. Since stress concentration decays with exactly that distance, the SDF hands the single most important variable to the model directly.

Output · 3 × 192 × 384

σxx  ·  σyy  ·  σxy

The three in-plane stress components, each divided by the nominal stress σgross.

Von Mises is not predicted directly. It is a nonlinear function of these three, so predicting the components lets us both derive it and test the prediction against equilibrium. Predicting von Mises alone would discard the information needed for that check. Dividing by σgross also makes the model transferable to any load and thickness.

Grid resolution: 384 × 192 at 0.52 mm per pixel
Chosen by measurement, not convention. Two different quantities were tracked across hole sizes:
field information (round-trip: grid → interpolate back to FE nodes) 256×128 0.19–0.39 % 384×192 0.13–0.26 % 512×256 0.09–0.19 % peak retained (grid maximum versus the true FE maximum) 256×128 ~5.0 % lost 384×192 ~2.6 % lost 512×256 ~2.6 % (noisy)
The field is already well captured at the coarser grid; what the finer grid buys is the peak. The peak sits exactly on the hole boundary, where no pixel centre can sit, so a fixed share of it is lost by any pixel grid — refining past 384 stops helping and starts jittering with grid alignment. The residual ~2.6% is a representation floor, not a solver error, and it is carried through to Section 06.
05

How performance is measured

Every metric defined; two of the three kept deliberately out of the loss
Masked averaging — the convention behind every number below
The canvas is a fixed physical window, so how much of it a plate covers varies per case. Every average is taken over material pixels only.
M = { pixels where mask = 1 } |M| = number of such pixels
This is not cosmetic. An identical model with a uniform 0.10 error reads as 0.095 on an in-distribution case (9% of the canvas empty) and 0.078 on the shorter out-of-distribution plate (39% empty) if the empty pixels are averaged in — the model would appear to improve out of distribution, purely because more of its pixels are free. Masking removes that artefact from both the loss and the metrics.
nRMSE — field accuracy
Root-mean-square error over the field, normalised by the nominal applied stress so it reads as a percentage and is comparable across cases.
σgross = F / (b · t) = 10 MPa nominal stress, identical for every case yi = σi / σgross the stored, dimensionless target nRMSE = 100 · sqrt( Σi∈M ( ŷi − yi )² / |M| ) [%]
σgross is a fixed yardstick, the same for all 545 cases. Normalising by each case’s own peak instead would reward the hardest cases with a larger denominator; normalising by the net-section stress would change the ruler with every hole size.
Kt — the engineering answer
The stress concentration factor: peak stress at the hole divided by the stress in the net section that remains beside it. This is the number a designer actually uses.
σvM = sqrt( σxx² − σxxσyy + σyy² + 3σxy² ) plane-stress von Mises σnet = F / ( (b − 2r) · t ) stress across the reduced section Kt = max( σvM over the hole boundary ) / σnet
Kt is reported against two references, and they answer different questions. Versus the label asks whether the network reproduced what it was shown. Versus the FE truth (stored per case, independent of any grid) asks how far the answer is from reality. The gap between the two is the export grid’s representation floor. Crucially, Kt was kept out of the training loss: a metric you have optimised is no longer independent evidence.
Equilibrium residual — a physics check the model never saw
A real stress field must balance forces at every interior point. This is computed on the predicted field by finite differences, and it was never part of training.
static equilibrium, no body force: ∂σxx/∂x + ∂σxy/∂y = 0 ∂σxy/∂x + ∂σyy/∂y = 0 residual = mean | div σ | / median | grad σ | interior pixels only
Only pixels whose four neighbours are all material are scored, so the stencil never straddles the hole boundary. The FEA labels themselves score 0.295 on this measure — that is the floor set by finite differences on interpolated data, and the reference against which the model’s value should be read.

The training loss was the masked mean-squared error on the three stress components and nothing else. Whether a plain field loss is enough to get the peak right is a question this baseline exists to answer — and Section 06 shows that it is not.

07

Limits — read this before using it

Three, in order of how likely they are to bite you
LIMIT 01

It fails silently outside its training envelope

On a 150 × 100 plate — the same physics, a different proportion — field error rises from 1.0% to 25.7% and the Kt bias flips sign from −4.6% to +18.9%. The model produces a plausible-looking field that is wrong, and it gives no signal of its own that anything is amiss.

Mitigation available today
The equilibrium residual rose to 0.858 against ~0.5 in-distribution, so it did detect this failure without needing ground truth. It can be computed on any prediction and used as a trust gate.
Honest caveat
It is a coarse detector. It did not flag the large-hole case, which scored 0.385 — lower than the test split — despite being three times less accurate.
Operating rule
Use only for 200 × 100 plates with 8 ≤ r ≤ 26 mm. Outside that, run the solver.
LIMIT 02

It under-predicts peak stress by about 4.6%

On unseen in-distribution cases the peak is systematically low. For a fatigue calculation, an unconservative peak is the worst direction to be wrong in. The error decomposes cleanly, and only part of it is the model’s fault:

CNN versus its own label 2.17 % the network smooths the peak export grid representation 3.02 % the peak sits between pixels ————————————————————————————————————— total versus FE truth 4.58 % measured on the test split
Why the model half happens
Pixels above 90% of the peak are ~0.04% of the domain and contribute ~0.5% of a plain MSE. The optimiser has almost no incentive to get them right, and convolution plus downsampling actively smooths them.
Worst affected
Small holes. The five worst test cases all have r = 8–11 mm, yet their field error is 0.55–0.98% — the field is fine, only the peak is wrong.
Interim guidance
Apply a +5% correction to predicted Kt, or treat the prediction as a screening value and confirm the shortlist with the solver.
LIMIT 03

The speed-up is 29×, not 1000×

16.5 ms per prediction on a laptop GPU against 480 ms for the complete FEA chain. Real, but modest — because this 2D problem is already cheap to solve. The value here is the pattern, not the ratio: the same pipeline applied to a 3D model that takes minutes per run is where the economics change.

Where it already pays
Optimisation loops and sensitivity studies with thousands of evaluations: 29× turns eight minutes into sixteen seconds.
Where it does not
One-off analyses. Running the solver is simpler and exact.
On CPU
129 ms per case — still 3.7× faster, if no GPU is available.
08

Where we go next

Four candidates. Each answers one question and can be run this week
PATH A

Magnitude-weighted loss

~30 min

Attacks the 2.17 pt model-attributable share of the peak under-prediction — the “CNN versus its own label” line in Limit 02. It cannot touch the 3.02 pt grid floor, which needs a finer export, not a better loss.

today L = Σi∈M ( ŷi − yi )² / |M| proposed L = Σi∈M wi ( ŷi − yi )² / Σi∈M wi wi = 1 + α · ( σvM,i / max σvM )p α = 4, p = 2 a pixel at the peak gets weight 5; one at 20% of the peak gets 1.16. the peak region's share of the loss rises from ~0.5% to ~3%.
Question it answers
Is the peak bias a loss-design problem, or a capacity problem?
Success criterion
Kt bias versus label moves from −2.17% toward zero while field nRMSE degrades by no more than ~20% relative.
Risk to watch
Over-weighting trades far-field accuracy for the peak. Both numbers get reported, so the trade is visible rather than hidden.
Sweep
α ∈ {2, 4, 8} against the fixed validation split, then a single final read on test.
PATH B

Train across plate proportions

~10 min generation + 30 min training

Tests whether the Limit 01 collapse is a data coverage problem — fixable by showing the model more shapes — or an encoding problem that needs a second SDF channel for the plate boundary.

trained today a × b = 200 × 100 aspect ratio a/b = 2.0 only collapses on a × b = 150 × 100 a/b = 1.5 add to TRAINING 150×100, 175×100, 250×100, 300×100 a/b = 1.5, 1.75, 2.5, 3.0 ~120 cases each, b fixed at 100 as the reference length new held-out set 125×100 a/b = 1.25, outside the trained range
Why these four
They bracket the failing ratio on both sides and extend beyond it, so the result separates interpolation from extrapolation.
Why b stays at 100
Dimensional analysis: a/b is the only additional ratio. Varying a alone spans it, and keeps the reference length fixed for the SDF scaling.
If it works
The operating envelope widens to a stated range of proportions, with a measured extrapolation margin.
If it does not
The next move is an input change — a distance field to the plate boundary alongside the hole SDF — not more data.
PATH C

Four times the data

~25 min generation

505 cases give a typical nearest-neighbour spacing of about 1/14 of each axis in the three-parameter space. Going to 2000 halves that. The question is whether the small-hole peak error is data-limited at all.

Question it answers
Is the bottleneck sample density, model capacity, or grid resolution?
Sequencing
Run after A and B. If weighting alone fixes the peak, more data was never the constraint and the extra 600 MB buys nothing.
Cost
~25 min of solving, ~1.8 GB of tensors, ~90 min of training.
PATH D

Ship the trust gate

~half a day

Limit 01’s mitigation is currently a number in a report. Making it a guardrail in the inference path is what turns a demo into something an engineer can use without reading this deck first.

What ships
Every prediction returns its equilibrium residual and an in-envelope check on (a, b, r). Out-of-envelope or high-residual requests fall through to the solver automatically.
Calibration
Set the residual threshold from the observed in-distribution distribution, the same way the free-surface tolerance was set from measurement rather than assumption.
Known gap
The residual missed the large-hole degradation, so the envelope check carries most of the weight. Both are needed.

Recommended order: A and B in parallel — they answer independent questions and together determine whether C is worth running at all. D is independent of the model work and can proceed alongside.
